name: Ginseng Ficus Bonsai
secondary_keywords: is ficus ginseng toxic to cats
question_title: How do you care for a ficus ginseng bonsai in the UAE?
quick_answer: Ficus ginseng care in the UAE comes down to steady conditions: give the bonsai plenty of bright light, water when the top part of the soil has dried, and keep it out of cold AC draughts. This ficus bonsai (Ficus microcarpa 'Ginseng') drops leaves when it is moved, chilled, overwatered or left too dry.

quick_facts.label: Light
quick_facts.value: Lots of bright light, close to a window. Filter harsh summer afternoon sun through glass.

quick_facts.label: Water
quick_facts.value: When the top part of the soil feels dry. Never leave the pot standing in water.

quick_facts.label: Temperature
quick_facts.value: Most ficus prefer about 16–29 °C (University of Missouri Extension). Keep it away from cold draughts.

quick_facts.label: Humidity
quick_facts.value: Average indoor humidity is fine (University of Missouri Extension). High humidity is preferable and helps aerial roots form (NC State Extension).

quick_facts.label: AC tolerance
quick_facts.value: Good in an AC room, but cold air blowing on the leaves causes yellowing and leaf drop.

quick_facts.label: Outdoors in UAE
quick_facts.value: Possible in shade from October to April; bring it in on nights below about 16 °C. In summer a small bonsai pot dries out fast in the heat.

quick_facts.label: Pets
quick_facts.value: Toxic to cats and dogs if chewed (ASPCA genus entry, Ficus sp.). The milky sap can irritate skin.

quick_facts.label: Growth
quick_facts.value: Fast for a bonsai. Prune the shoots to keep the shape.

quick_facts.label: Main problem
quick_facts.value: Leaf drop after a move, a cold draught or a watering mistake.

good_if: You want your first bonsai: NC State Extension calls the ginseng ficus easier to care for than other bonsai.
You have a bright spot near a window in an AC home or office.
You enjoy small, regular jobs such as pruning shoots and checking the soil.
You want a desk or table plant with a sculptural trunk and roots.
think_twice: A cat or dog in your home chews plants: ficus is toxic if eaten.
Your only space is a dim corner or a spot right under an AC vent.
You travel often and cannot check a small pot that dries out quickly.
You will be upset by some leaf drop when the plant moves to a new spot.

care_sections.heading: How much light does a ficus ginseng bonsai need?
paragraphs: A ficus ginseng bonsai needs plenty of light. University of Missouri Extension says the first key to a healthy indoor ficus is lots of light, from a good east-, west- or south-facing window or from plant lights. NC State Extension lists full sun to part shade for the species, Ficus microcarpa, and says to keep a ginseng ficus in a sunny, warm location.

A ficus ginseng in a dim room drops its leaves: UF/IFAS Extension lists low light as a cause of green leaf drop and says to move the plant to a brighter spot. Ficus is sensitive to sudden changes in light, so make any move to a much brighter or darker place gradually.

In the UAE, strong afternoon sun through west- or south-facing glass in summer can dry and shrivel ficus leaves. UF/IFAS lists too much sunlight as a cause of dry, shrivelled leaves. A sheer curtain filters that sun and keeps the light bright.

care_sections.heading: How often should you water a ficus ginseng bonsai?
paragraphs: Water a ficus ginseng bonsai when the top part of the soil has dried, not on a fixed day. Extension sources word this in two ways: NC State Extension says to keep a ginseng ficus consistently moist, and UF/IFAS Extension says the potting mix should be kept moist. University of Missouri Extension advises watering when the top 25 to 50 percent of the potting mix is dry to the touch, and warns that too much water suffocates the roots. Together they mean: keep the soil below the surface evenly moist, never soggy and never bone dry.

To test a ficus ginseng bonsai, push a finger or a wooden skewer into the soil. If the upper part is dry and the soil below is only just damp, water. If the soil is still wet near the surface, wait and test again later.

How fast ficus ginseng soil dries depends on the pot and the room. A small or shallow bonsai pot holds little soil and dries faster than a deep pot. A warm, bright window, inland heat and outdoor summer air dry the soil quickly; a dim AC room, a glazed pot and humid coastal weather keep it damp for longer. In the cooler months growth slows and the soil takes longer to dry.

When you water, water thoroughly until water runs out of the drainage hole, then empty the saucer or cover pot once it stops dripping. Both a soil that stays wet and a soil that dries out completely make a ficus drop leaves, so steady watering matters more than the amount.
tips: UF/IFAS lists moisture stress as a cause of yellow leaf drop. If leaves fall soon after the soil went bone dry or stayed soggy, adjust the watering first.
If you see a white crust on the soil or pot, flush the pot with plenty of water to wash out the salts.

care_sections.heading: What soil and pot does a ficus ginseng bonsai need?
paragraphs: A ficus ginseng bonsai needs a potting mix that holds some water but drains well. UF/IFAS Extension says ficus needs a mix with good water-holding capacity and aeration, made from ingredients such as peat, pine bark and perlite. NC State Extension lists good drainage for the species.

Extra water must be able to leave the pot, because NC State Extension names overwatering as a cause of root rot in Ficus microcarpa. A pot with a drainage hole is the easiest way. If the bonsai sits in a decorative bowl or cover pot, empty any water that collects at the bottom after watering.

care_sections.heading: Can a ficus ginseng bonsai live with AC in the UAE?
paragraphs: Yes, a ficus ginseng bonsai grows well in an air-conditioned UAE home or office, as long as cold air does not blow on it. University of Missouri Extension says most ficus prefer about 16–29 °C (60–85 °F), and that air noticeably warmer or cooler than the room causes leaf yellowing and leaf drop. UF/IFAS Extension says to avoid draughts.

To check a spot for a ficus bonsai, turn the AC on and hold your hand next to the leaves. If you feel the air moving, move the bonsai further away or turn the louvres away from it. Heaters and warm air from appliances cause the same problem.

Average indoor humidity is fine for a ficus, according to University of Missouri Extension. NC State Extension says high humidity (70–100%) is preferable for Ficus microcarpa and seems to favour the aerial roots that hang from its branches.

care_sections.heading: Should you fertilise a ficus ginseng bonsai?
paragraphs: Yes, a ficus ginseng bonsai benefits from feeding while it grows. University of Missouri Extension says ficus can be fed as little as once or twice a year or as often as the fertiliser label recommends, and that most gardeners stop in winter, when light levels fall and the days get shorter. In the UAE, pause feeding in the short days of winter and start again when new growth appears in spring.

Too much fertiliser builds up salts in a small bonsai pot. UF/IFAS Extension links high salts to loss of the oldest leaves, stunted growth and shrivelled roots, and advises less fertiliser, water with low salts and flushing the soil. Yellowing leaf edges point the other way, to underfeeding.

care_sections.heading: How do you prune a ficus ginseng bonsai?
paragraphs: Prune a ficus ginseng bonsai by cutting back long shoots, thinning crowded branches and removing dead twigs, so that it keeps its shape. NC State Extension describes it as a fast grower, and UF/IFAS Extension says ficus usually needs pruning to keep its shape, to thin the foliage so light gets inside, and to remove dead branches.
Ficus has a milky sap (latex). NC State Extension says it can cause minor skin irritation, especially in sunlight, so wear gloves if your skin is sensitive and keep the sap away from pets.
steps: Use clean, sharp scissors or shears. UF/IFAS advises sterilised shears for removing dead twigs.
Cut back long shoots that spoil the outline of the canopy.
Thin crowded branches inside the canopy so light reaches the inner leaves.
Remove dead twigs and any curled, folded leaves (a sign of thrips).
Do not prune a new plant straight away. Let it settle in its new spot first.

care_sections.heading: When should you repot a ficus ginseng bonsai?
paragraphs: Repot a ficus ginseng bonsai when the roots fill the pot or water runs straight through. University of Missouri Extension says repotting every year or two gives the best growth under ideal conditions, and that ficus tolerates being root-bound but does not prefer it.

Do not repot a ficus ginseng in its first weeks at home. UF/IFAS Extension advises not to move, prune, repot or fertilise a ficus for at least about four weeks after it is placed indoors. In the UAE, most repotting is done in the cooler months, from October to April.
Keep the thick ginseng roots at the same height as before when you repot. The roots are the feature of a ficus ginseng, so do not bury them deeper in the new soil.

care_sections.heading: Can you propagate a ficus ginseng?
paragraphs: Yes. NC State Extension says Ficus microcarpa propagates easily from cuttings, either in water or directly in sand or potting soil.

care_sections.heading: Can a ficus ginseng bonsai live outside in the UAE?
paragraphs: A ficus ginseng bonsai can go outside in shade during the cooler months. NC State Extension lists Ficus microcarpa for full sun to part shade and for climates that stay warm all year, but a bonsai in a small pot has little soil and dries out quickly in UAE summer heat.

From May to September, keep an outdoor bonsai in shade and test the soil more often, or bring it indoors. Move it between an AC room and the outdoors gradually, because ficus reacts to sudden changes in light and temperature with leaf drop. In winter, bring an outdoor bonsai indoors on nights below about 16 °C: UF/IFAS Extension says to keep ficus above 60 °F (about 16 °C) at all times to avoid chilling injury, which shows as slimy dark spots and mass leaf drop. These nights are common inland (Al Ain, desert areas) and in colder GCC cities, and also happen on the coast in January.

varieties.name: Ginseng ficus (single tree)
varieties.look: Thick, swollen roots above the soil, a short trunk and a canopy of glossy, teardrop-shaped leaves
varieties.best_for: Desks, shelves and first-time bonsai owners

varieties.name: Grafted ginseng ficus
varieties.look: Ginseng roots with branches of a smaller-leaved ficus grafted on top
varieties.best_for: A finer, more tree-like bonsai look

varieties.look: A taller bonsai with a curved trunk and a dense, clipped canopy
varieties.care: Same care. A bigger pot dries out more slowly than a small bonsai pot.
varieties.best_for: Living rooms, receptions and office tables

first_week.intro: A ficus ginseng bonsai often drops some leaves after delivery as it adjusts to new light and temperature. The best help in the first weeks is a steady spot and careful watering.
steps: Put the bonsai in a bright spot near a window, out of harsh afternoon sun and away from AC vents.
Leave it in that spot. Ficus reacts to every move, so do not keep moving it around.
Test the soil before the first watering, and water only when the top part feels dry.
Do not repot, prune or feed yet. UF/IFAS Extension advises waiting at least about four weeks after a ficus is placed indoors.
Pick up fallen leaves and watch the new growth. If leaves keep falling after the first weeks, check the light, the draughts and the soil.

uae_year.care: Indoors under AC a ficus ginseng keeps growing: test the soil before you water and keep the bonsai out of cold air from vents and out of harsh afternoon sun through glass. Outdoor bonsai need shade, and small pots dry out fast in the heat, so test them more often or bring them in.
A good time to repot a root-bound ficus ginseng and to move bonsai back to shaded balconies (gradually). From November growth slows and the soil takes longer to dry.

A ficus ginseng grows more slowly in winter: water only when the soil tests dry and stop feeding. Nights below about 16 °C (60 °F, the temperature UF/IFAS Extension says to keep ficus above) are common inland (Al Ain, desert areas) and in Riyadh or Kuwait, and also happen on the coast in January: bring outdoor bonsai indoors on cold nights. Make sure outdoor pots drain after rain.
Start feeding a ficus ginseng bonsai again and prune long shoots to keep the shape. Spring is the second window for repotting. Move outdoor bonsai into shade before May.

problems.question: Why is my ficus ginseng bonsai dropping leaves?
problems.cause: A move, a draught, cold, low light or a watering mistake
problems.answer: A ficus ginseng drops leaves when its conditions change or stress it. University of Missouri Extension names changes in its surroundings, cold and uneven watering, and UF/IFAS Extension adds soil that stays too wet and low light. Some leaf drop after delivery or a move is normal; it is a problem only if it continues.
problems.signs: Leaves falling soon after a move, next to an AC vent or window, or after the soil stayed wet or went bone dry.
fix: Keep the bonsai in one bright spot and stop moving it.
Check for cold or warm air blowing on it, and move it out of the airflow.
Test the soil: if it is wet, let it dry before you water again; if it is bone dry, water thoroughly.
If the room is dim, move the plant gradually to a brighter place.
Wait for new leaves. A ficus that keeps its new growth has settled.

problems.question: Why are my ficus ginseng leaves turning yellow while the soil stays wet?
problems.symptom: Yellow leaves, soil that stays wet
problems.answer: Yellow leaves on a ficus ginseng whose soil stays wet usually mean too much water. NC State Extension names overwatering as a cause of root rot in Ficus microcarpa, and University of Missouri Extension says too much water suffocates the roots.
problems.signs: Soil still wet days after watering, water left in the bowl or cover pot, a sour smell, dark soft roots.
fix: Stop watering and empty any water from the saucer or cover pot.
Lift the bonsai out of its pot and look at the roots.
Cut off black, soft roots with clean scissors.
Repot in fresh, well-drained mix in a pot with a drainage hole.
Water again only when the top part of the soil tests dry.

problems.question: Why are the new leaves on my ficus ginseng curled, folded and spotted purple?
problems.symptom: New leaves folded with purple or brown scars
problems.answer: New leaves that curl and fold along the middle vein, with dark brown, reddish or purplish scars, are galls made by Cuban laurel thrips. University of California IPM says this thrips mainly attacks Ficus microcarpa. Small black insects and pale larvae live inside the folded leaves. The damage is mostly cosmetic, but heavy feeding can slow growth and make leaves fall early.
problems.signs: Folded new leaves, purple or brown scars, tiny black insects inside the fold.
fix: Move the bonsai away from other ficus plants.
Cut off the curled, folded leaves and shoot tips and throw them away in a closed bag.
Check new leaves as they open and remove any that fold.
If the galls keep coming back, ask about a systemic insecticide labelled for thrips on houseplants. Sprays on the outside of the leaf do not reach thrips inside the galls.

problems.question: What are the white specks and fine webs on my ficus ginseng?
problems.symptom: White flecks on leaves, fine webbing
problems.answer: Tiny white flecks on ficus leaves, sometimes with fine webbing, are a sign of spider mites. NC State Extension lists spider mites as a pest of Ficus microcarpa, and Colorado State University Extension says their feeding wounds appear as white flecks.
problems.signs: Pale, speckled leaves; fine webs between leaves and stems; leaf drop in bad cases.
fix: Wash the whole plant with a jet of water from a shower or kitchen sprayer, including the leaf undersides.
Repeat the wash until no new flecks or webs appear.
Raise the humidity around the plant: Colorado State University Extension names washing and higher humidity as the most effective controls.
For a bad infestation, use a houseplant spray such as a neem-based product or horticultural oil, following the label.

problems.question: Why are my ficus ginseng leaves sticky, with brown bumps or white fluff?
problems.symptom: Sticky leaves, brown bumps or white cotton
problems.answer: Sticky leaves with small brown bumps on the stems and leaf veins are a sign of scale insects; white, cottony clusters are mealybugs. NC State Extension lists both as pests of Ficus microcarpa. Both suck sap and leave a sticky honeydew on the leaves below.
problems.signs: Brown or grey bumps that do not move, white fluff in leaf joints, sticky leaves, weak growth.
fix: Move the bonsai away from other plants.
Rub or pick off scale insects where there are only a few.
Dab mealybugs with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Spray the plant with horticultural oil or a neem-based houseplant spray, following the label, and repeat as the label allows.

problems.question: Why are my ficus ginseng leaves dry and shrivelled?
problems.cause: Too much sun or very low humidity
problems.answer: Dry, shrivelled leaves on a ficus ginseng come from too much sunlight or very low humidity, according to UF/IFAS Extension. In the UAE this can happen when a bonsai sits in afternoon sun behind glass or outdoors in summer without shade.
problems.signs: Dry, crisp leaves on the side facing the sun, often after a move to a sunnier spot.
fix: Move the bonsai out of harsh direct sun or filter it with a sheer curtain.
Check that the soil is not drying out completely between waterings.
Keep it away from hot or cold air from vents and appliances.
The damaged leaves will not recover. Remove them and wait for new growth.

mistakes.mistake: Watering on a fixed weekly schedule
mistakes.instead: Water when the top part of the soil is dry. Test it with a finger or a skewer before each watering.

mistakes.mistake: Water left standing in the bonsai bowl, saucer or cover pot
mistakes.instead: Water until it drains, then empty the saucer or cover pot once the pot stops dripping.

mistakes.mistake: A spot right under or in front of an AC vent
mistakes.instead: Keep the bonsai out of the airflow. With the AC on, hold your hand next to the leaves: if you feel moving air, move the plant or turn the louvres away.

mistakes.mistake: Moving the bonsai again and again to find the right spot
mistakes.instead: Choose one bright spot and leave the plant there. Every move can cause new leaf drop.

mistakes.mistake: Repotting, pruning and feeding a new bonsai straight away
mistakes.instead: Let it settle first. UF/IFAS Extension advises waiting at least about four weeks after a ficus is placed indoors.

mistakes.mistake: Burying the thick ginseng roots when you repot
mistakes.instead: Keep the roots at the same height as before. They are the feature of the plant.

mistakes.mistake: A dim corner far from any window
mistakes.instead: Bright light near a window, or a plant light. Low light causes leaf drop.

myths.myth: A ficus ginseng is a ginseng plant.
myths.fact: A ficus ginseng is a fig, Ficus microcarpa. It gets its name from its thick, swollen roots, which look like ginseng roots.

myths.myth: Leaf drop means the bonsai is dying.
myths.fact: Ficus often drops leaves after a move or a change in conditions. University of Missouri Extension says this is not necessarily a problem unless it continues over time.
UF/IFAS Extension says Ficus microcarpa is grown as a tree outdoors in the tropics but is commonly used as a bonsai indoors. A ficus ginseng does well indoors in bright light.

myths.myth: A bonsai on your desk cleans the air in the room.
myths.fact: A 2019 review of chamber studies found that a building would need 10 to 1,000 potted plants per square metre of floor to match the air exchange it already has. Keep a bonsai because you enjoy it, not as an air cleaner.

pet_safety.summary: No, a ficus ginseng bonsai is not pet-safe. The ASPCA has no separate entry for Ficus microcarpa, but its genus entry for fig plants (Weeping Fig, Ficus sp.) is toxic to cats, dogs and horses, with the toxic principles ficin and ficusin. For weeping fig (Ficus benjamina), the ASPCA lists stomach and skin irritation as the signs, and Clemson Extension says all parts are irritating, especially the white, milky sap. Keep the bonsai out of reach of pets and young children.
pet_safety.emergency: Call your vet or a 24-hour animal emergency clinic straight away and tell them the plant name (ficus, Ficus microcarpa). Do not wait for symptoms.

faqs.q: Is a ficus ginseng the same as Ficus retusa?
faqs.a: Ginseng ficus is often sold labelled Ficus retusa, but NC State Extension says that is a common mislabel: the ginseng ficus is a cultivar of Ficus microcarpa, and the name Ficus retusa belongs to another plant. So a ginseng bonsai labelled 'Ficus retusa' is still a Ficus microcarpa and follows the advice in this guide.

faqs.q: Is a ficus ginseng a good bonsai for beginners?
faqs.a: Yes. NC State Extension says the ginseng ficus grows somewhat faster and is easier to care for than other bonsai species, which makes it a good first bonsai. It needs bright light, steady watering and a spot out of draughts more than special bonsai skills.

faqs.q: Does a ficus ginseng clean the air?
faqs.a: A ficus ginseng does not noticeably clean the air in a normal room. A 2019 review of chamber studies (Cummings and Waring) found that a building would need 10 to 1,000 potted plants per square metre of floor to match the air exchange it already gets from ventilation.

faqs.q: Why is it called a ginseng ficus?
faqs.a: A ginseng ficus is named after its thick, bulbous roots, which look like ginseng roots. NC State Extension says these exposed roots are the reason the cultivar is used so widely for bonsai. It is a fig, not a ginseng plant.

faqs.q: Why does my ficus ginseng grow thin roots from its branches?
faqs.a: Thin roots that hang from the branches are aerial roots, which are normal for Ficus microcarpa. NC State Extension says high humidity favours them. You can leave them or remove them: University of Missouri Extension says unwanted aerial roots can be removed without harming the plant.

faqs.q: How big does a ficus ginseng bonsai get?
faqs.a: A ficus ginseng bonsai stays small because it grows in a small pot and is pruned regularly. The same species, Ficus microcarpa, grows into a large tree in warm climates: NC State Extension says it can reach about 12 m (40 ft) outdoors in Mediterranean climates.

faqs.q: Is the sap of a ficus ginseng harmful to people?
faqs.a: The white, milky sap (latex) of a ficus can irritate the skin. NC State Extension says ficus latex can cause minor skin irritation, especially in sunlight. Wear gloves when you prune if your skin is sensitive, wash your hands afterwards, and keep the plant away from young children who might chew it.

faqs.q: Is a ficus ginseng bonsai a good gift?
faqs.a: A ficus ginseng bonsai suits people who have a bright window and enjoy small care jobs such as pruning. Tell the person that some leaf drop in the first weeks is normal, and that the plant is toxic to cats and dogs.
